extracted.intended_audience: researchers, scientometricians, and research-funding agency staff interested in validating peer review and assessing research impact
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and interpreting studies that test whether ex-ante peer review (scores or funding decisions) predicts later research impact and related outcomes. Focuses on choice of impact metrics, study design (controls, timing), internal validity of review, and contextual interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of multiple impact metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Including a panel of indicators is likely to give a clearer picture of impact (Hicks et al., 2015) and allows sensitivity to the multidimensional aspects of research impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators still need qualitative interpretation in the context of the science and funding program (Chen, 2016). Strike a balance between comprehensiveness and feasibility (Milat et al., 2015). Examples: Melin and Danell (2006) found funded applicants published in higher quality journals and received more external funding, spin-offs, and patents despite similar publication counts. Use multiple indicators because some measures may show predictive validity while others do not; integration methods and relative weights matter (Lee, 2015; Milat et al., 2015).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decouple the effects of funding itself from review decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Future studies need to de-couple the effects of funding itself from the review decision before metrics can truly test review validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex-post differences may result from having received funding (resources/opportunities), not necessarily from the correctness of the review decision. Design studies that can separate causal effects of funding from selection effects (e.g., via appropriate controls, natural experiments, or quasi-experimental designs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include unfunded control groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies must compare funded applicants/projects to similarly qualified unfunded applicants/projects; lacking an unfunded control limits ability to test validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review found 29% of studies lacked an unfunded control; among studies with unfunded controls, 91% showed some level of predictive validity. Without unfunded controls, interpreting ex-post differences is problematic because funding may cause the difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for ex-ante applicant/project qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust for pre-application (ex-ante) qualifications because differences in outcomes can diminish when ex-ante qualifications are accounted for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several studies (e.g., Pion and Cordray, 2008) showed that effects (e.g., securing faculty positions) were diminished when adjusted for ex-ante qualifications. Include measures of prior productivity/quality in analyses to avoid confounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an appropriate impact time window (account for latency)
rubrics_metrics.description: The time window when impact is measured, especially for bibliometric impact, is an important variable; the median maximum time in bibliometric studies was around 5 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different results can emerge at <=5 years vs. >5 years. Select a time window appropriate to the discipline and outcome (e.g., patents and societal impact may take longer). Report sensitivity to different time windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely solely on bibliometric measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Bibliometric measures dominate but have many issues and can depend on factors unrelated to research quality; many evaluations rely only on bibliometrics, which is limiting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplement bibliometrics with non-bibliometric data (project initiation/completion, patents, technology licensing, post-project peer review, international collaboration, future funding success, securing tenure track positions, career satisfaction). Consider altmetrics and field-appropriate citation targets (e.g., clinical guidelines for clinical research).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret indicators in program- and discipline-specific context
rubrics_metrics.description: Integration and interpretation of indicators must consider the area of science, goals of the research program, and how excellence was defined and operationalized in the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different programs have different goals and may evolve over time; subjective definitions of excellence may not equate to innovation or impact (Luukkonen, 2012). Contextualize findings by program goals, funding mechanisms, and reviewer instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for variability and noise in bibliometric indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Bibliometric indicators can show a large degree of variability, especially at the project level, which can obscure correlations and firm conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of high variance, bibliometric measures should be supplemented and robustness checks performed; caution against over-interpreting small effect sizes. Use normalization and appropriate statistical methods to handle variability (Bornmann et al., 2008a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the incentives and feedback effects of impact assessment on reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of impact assessment on funding incentives is non-trivial and likely influences ex-ante peer review decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that how impact is measured may alter researcher behavior and reviewer judgments (Lindner and Nakamura, 2015; Bornmann, 2017). When validating peer review, consider how the choice of indicators creates incentives that feed back into the review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance comprehensiveness and feasibility when selecting indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a 'right balance between comprehensiveness and feasibility' when determining how many and what type of indicators to include (Milat et al., 2015).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very comprehensive frameworks (e.g., Payback) capture long-term and multiple outcome categories but are labor-intensive and may be less relevant to assessing individual projects. Select panels of indicators that are feasible to collect and appropriate to the evaluation purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine qualitative and quantitative evaluation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Holistic evaluation frameworks should involve qualitative and quantitative aspects of research quality and impact as well as peer and end-user evaluation to capture public value of research (Donovan, 2007).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interviews, case studies, stakeholder feedback, and expert judgment alongside metrics to assess outcomes that bibliometrics miss (e.g., policy influence, practice change).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight and integrate indicators thoughtfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Just as reviewers weigh relative importance of review criteria, how one weighs indicators into an overall picture of impact is crucial (Lee, 2015; Milat et al., 2015).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop explicit weighting or integration strategies and justify them relative to program goals; perform sensitivity analyses to weighting choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure societal impact and productive stakeholder interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitating productive interactions between scientists and stakeholders is proposed as a key generator of societal impact, though more studies are needed to confirm assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider indicators of engagement, policy uptake, technology transfer, spin-offs, and other societal outcomes. Use frameworks and instruments (e.g., Sarli et al., 2010; Luke et al., 2018) to operationalize these measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use frameworks like the Payback framework for long-term and multi-source attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The Payback framework gauges outcomes derived from over a decade of investment and accounts for latency and attribution to multiple sources (Donovan, 2011).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payback integrates knowledge creation, future research benefits, political benefits, health sector benefits and economic benefits; good practice for comprehensive evaluation but resource-intensive and possibly less suited to individual-project assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess internal validity of peer review: inter-rater reliability and reviewer effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal validity tests of the review process—examining reviewer bias, review structures, baselines of decision making and inter-rater reliability—are crucial for assessing fairness, efficiency, and rationality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many studies indicate low inter-rater reliability and reviewer-dependent scores; include analyses of rater variance, panel effects, and how discussions change outcomes (Carpenter et al., 2015). Such internal tests were not the focus of the reviewed studies but are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid restricting analysis to narrow score ranges or excluding poorer-scoring cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When poorer scoring unfunded applicants or poorer scoring projects are excluded, observed validity often disappears, depending on metric used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the full range of scores and ensure inclusion of lower-scoring projects where relevant to detect discriminatory power across the spectrum. Beware analyses limited to top-tier applicants only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for selection biases including the Matthew effect
rubrics_metrics.description: For studies using ex-ante performance as a predictor, they should take into account the Matthew effect, since funding less-awarded groups may have higher impact than more distinguished groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret findings with awareness that cumulative advantage can bias estimates; use designs/controls that mitigate or explicitly model Matthew effects (Langfeldt et al., 2015; Mongeon et al., 2016).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer study designs that enable causal inference (ex-ante vs ex-post comparisons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examining ex-post applicant performance without comparing ex-ante performance may fail to remove the effect of funding itself; ex-ante measures are needed to test prediction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design studies that compare pre-application metrics and control for baseline differences, or use randomized, regression discontinuity, or matched designs where feasible to strengthen causal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include measures beyond traditional outputs, e.g., reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: As reproducibility is important, assessments of reproducibility (e.g., the r-factor) are in development and should be considered as impact indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider including reproducibility and transparency metrics alongside citations and patents as part of a modern impact panel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious using citation-per-dollar or cost-normalized metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation level per dollar spent (citation per dollar) can mask correlations and may distort interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that normalizing by cost can obscure relationships between scores and productivity; present both raw and cost-normalized analyses where relevant and interpret with caution (Danthi et al., 2014; Doyle et al., 2015).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiate and ensure access to pre-funding peer review data
rubrics_metrics.description: More research needs to be done to understand peer review validity, which means improved access to pre-funding peer review data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Academics should work with funding agencies to negotiate data access agreements; funding agencies should invest in validation studies and data sharing protocols to enable robust evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for inequality, randomness, anomalies and extreme events when measuring impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Most evaluations fail to consider inequality, random chance, anomalies, the right to make mistakes, unpredictability and extreme events—hallmarks of scientific process that likely distort measurements of impact (Bornmann, 2017).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design metrics and interpretation frameworks that acknowledge heavy-tailed impact distributions and the role of rare high-impact events; use robust statistics and report uncertainty and distributional characteristics.
